families.title: Run agents
families.blurb: Start, steer, pay for and hand over the agents themselves.

families.title: Organize the work
families.blurb: Projects, roles, teams, queues, workflows and schedules turn one-off prompts into a system.

families.title: Remember and review
families.blurb: What the fleet learned, what it produced, and the human check before it lands.

families.title: Connect and extend
families.blurb: Tools, secrets, desktop control, skills, hooks and other machines, with controls over what each can reach.

families.title: See and steer
families.blurb: One place to notice what needs you, look back at what ran, and work next to the agents.

categories.title: Agents you can steer mid-flight
categories.label: Agents
categories.short: Queue a note, steer now, pause, resume and compact a live session
categories.keywords: spawn send message force interrupt pause hold resume release compaction compact reconfigure settings kill worktree history sub-agent shadow fleet
categories.problem: A long agent run is a black box. You can wait, or you can kill it and lose the context it spent an hour building.
categories.benefit: Every running agent stays addressable. You can queue a note for its next turn, ask it to change course now, pause it with its conversation kept, change how it behaves, and let it compact its own context, all without throwing the session away.
categories.scenario: The Atlas conductor is mid-turn on a CSS refactor when you notice it is editing the wrong stylesheet. You send a forced message, which asks the backend to interrupt or steer the turn. Edits it already made stay on disk, so you review them. An hour later a quota window runs out, so you hold the agent and release it once the quota is back: the aborted turn is re-queued and runs again on the same conversation.

items.name: Claude or Codex, side by side
items.text: Spawn agents on either backend from the same cockpit; Kimi and generic OpenAI-compatible backends are also supported.

items.name: Next-turn or forced messages
items.text: A normal message waits for the next turn boundary. A forced one asks the backend to interrupt or steer the active turn; what the turn already did is not rolled back. Each send reports whether a turn started, is mid-turn, is pending or the agent is held.

items.name: Slash commands pass through
items.text: A message marked as a provider slash command, like /compact, arrives verbatim so the backend reads it as a command instead of as text.

items.name: Stall detection
items.text: If a message is delivered but no turn ever opens, the daemon raises a prompt-stalled event you can subscribe to.

items.name: Interrupt
items.text: Abort only the in-flight turn. The process stays up and addressable and can take new input.

items.name: Hold and release
items.text: Park an agent: its turn is aborted and re-queued, it does not wake on mail, and release resumes it with full context. Side effects the aborted turn already caused are not undone, and the docs say so.

items.name: Quota pauses stay put
items.text: A session-limit or crash-backoff pause is not released early by accident; you opt in when you know the quota is back.

items.name: Kill when you mean it
items.text: A real stop that ends the process, kept separate from interrupt and hold.

items.name: Reconfigure in one respawn
items.text: Change model, effort, account, turn limits, budget ceiling, compaction threshold, instructions or autonomy; the conversation survives and the next turn behaves the new way.

items.name: Live changes, no respawn
items.text: Permission profile and display label apply without interrupting a running turn.

items.name: Compaction on request
items.text: Ask an agent to compact its context. Claude receives /compact, Codex gets its native compact request, and completion arrives later as an event, because acceptance is not completion.

items.name: Hand off across providers
items.text: When a quota window is spent, move an agent's context to a fresh agent on another provider or account through a portable package of brief, anchors and recent turns.

items.name: Rebind to another directory
items.text: Move an agent to a new working directory with the same provider, account and model.

items.name: Provider remote control
items.text: Turn provider-native remote control on for a live session where the CLI and account support it.

items.name: Fleet dashboard and lanes
items.text: Agents grouped by team or project, with live status lanes and pinned tasks or agents that keep their live fields in view.

items.name: Native sub-agent rows
items.text: A provider's own sub-agents appear as read-only shadow rows with their task, summary and metrics.

items.name: Spawn cost preview
items.text: Estimate the token cost of the Chimera tool grant a spawn would get before you spawn it. It is an estimate, never a policy.

figure.alt: Chimera desktop app: agent sidebar with Claude and Codex agents on the demo project Atlas website, and an agent conversation with tool calls (demo data)
figure.caption: Actual Chimera interface · demo data

categories.title: Providers, accounts and failover
categories.label: Providers and failover
categories.short: Several accounts and providers, with failover when quota runs out
categories.keywords: provider account failover quota subscription keychain oauth api key claude codex kimi cooldown model catalog login custom model ollama lmstudio vllm openai-compatible override
categories.problem: One subscription has one quota. When it runs dry mid-task, everything waiting on it stops, and juggling logins by hand does not scale past a couple of agents.
categories.benefit: Register several accounts across providers and let Chimera route around an exhausted one, so a quota limit becomes a delay instead of a stall.
categories.scenario: Three Atlas workers share a Claude subscription that hits its session limit. The scheduler cools that account down and moves new work to your second account. When the quota resets you clear the cooldown in one action instead of editing config.

items.name: Several ways to log in
items.text: Subscription login, a key in the OS keychain, an environment variable, an external command that prints a key, or OAuth.

items.name: Test before you trust
items.text: Add, remove, re-key and test an account from the UI or through the account tools.

items.name: Cooldown and uncool
items.text: A spent account is cooled down; clearing it releases the agents that were paused on that account's session limit.

items.name: Across accounts
items.text: Work moves to another account of the same provider when one is exhausted.

items.name: Across providers, if you allow it
items.text: Failover can optionally cross providers; an agent can also be handed off to a fresh agent on another provider with its context.

items.name: Per-project conductor account
items.text: Pin the account, and optionally the model and permission profile, a project's conductor is born on.

items.name: Provider and model lists
items.text: Browse the providers and the models each exposes, then pick per role, per agent or per spawn.

items.name: Your own OpenAI-compatible server
items.text: Define a custom provider with a base URL and default model, for a local Ollama, LM Studio or vLLM server. A key is only asked for if you say the server needs one.

items.name: Base URL and default model overrides
items.text: Override a built-in provider's base URL or default model, and set a per-provider context-compaction threshold. Changes apply on the next daemon start.

items.name: Early-access note
items.text: Claude and Codex are the main paths. Kimi and the generic OpenAI-compatible backend are also available.

categories.title: Permissions, approvals and budgets
categories.label: Permissions and budgets
categories.short: Permission profiles, approvals and spend ceilings
categories.keywords: permission approval profile readonly acceptedits full budget ceiling usage cost slo host tools policy allow ask deny write gate
categories.problem: Agents that can edit files and run commands need limits, and limits only work if they are visible, adjustable mid-run and tied to real spend.
categories.benefit: Pick how much freedom an agent has, answer permission prompts from one place, and put a dollar ceiling on a whole tree of agents instead of watching a meter.
categories.scenario: A research sub-agent on Atlas starts under the read-only profile. When it asks to run a command, the request lands in your inbox; you allow it once. Later the whole spawn tree crosses its budget ceiling, so the tree pauses and tells you instead of quietly continuing.

items.name: Read-only, accept edits, full
items.text: Three profiles per backend, overridable per project or per spawn, and changeable on a live agent without a respawn.

items.name: Approvals in one feed
items.text: Pending permission requests show up in the attention inbox and can be answered allow or deny from there.

items.name: Single-writer write gate
items.text: A worktree has one writer at a time. A dry run tells you whether writing certain paths would be refused and why; the mode is enforce, warn or off.

items.name: Ceilings on a spawn tree
items.text: A budget covers a whole tree of agents. A breach pauses the tree. Budget warnings are an event you can subscribe to.

items.name: Per-agent ceilings
items.text: Set a maximum spend on one agent through reconfigure.

items.name: Usage and performance
items.text: Query usage, and read latency, tokens, cost, gate failures and error rates by team, provider or workflow.

items.name: Honest about estimates
items.text: Some budgets are estimated from token counts, not from a provider invoice.

items.name: Allow, ask or deny per CLI tool
items.text: Chimera scans the command-line tools on the host and keeps an allow, ask or deny policy per tool and profile, with a wildcard row.

categories.title: Voice and meetings
categories.label: Voice and meetings
categories.short: Talk to agents and run meeting rooms
categories.keywords: voice meeting room microphone codex push to talk transcription consent audio preview
categories.problem: Some conversations with an agent are faster spoken than typed, and some decisions need several agents and you in the same room.
categories.benefit: Talk to an agent on its existing authenticated session, or open a bounded meeting room with an approved roster. Consent is explicit and the coding work keeps running when audio ends.
categories.scenario: Before a refactor, you open a meeting room for the Atlas conductor and two workers. You approve the roster, set a duration and utterance budget, and give desktop consent. When the call ends, the coding work carries on.

items.name: Per-agent opt-in
items.text: Native Codex voice runs on an agent's existing authenticated thread, only for agents you opt in, with microphone consent in the desktop UI.

items.name: Push to talk
items.text: A separate path transcribes your speech to text for agents that have no native voice.

items.name: Approved roster
items.text: A room has a named roster; editing the roster renews consent.

items.name: Budgets
items.text: A duration and utterance budget bound each room.

items.name: Audio is separate from work
items.text: Ending audio does not stop agents' coding work. Create, list, update, end and delete rooms through the voice-room tools.

categories.limits: Voice is a preview. It needs the desktop app for microphone consent and is not part of the baseline workflow.

categories.title: Projects and conductors
categories.label: Projects and conductors
categories.short: Bind a repo to teams, a queue and an always-on conductor
categories.keywords: project conductor import clone assign team archive routing dispatch checkpoint session setup account
categories.problem: Real work lives in repositories. Without a project boundary, agents, queues and memory blur together and every new session starts cold.
categories.benefit: A project binds a repository to its teams, queue and conductor. Work routed to the project lands on the right team, with the right permissions and account.
categories.scenario: You import the Atlas website repository from a git URL, assign the web team, and start its conductor. A new task is dispatched to the project and lands on the bound queue instead of a random worker.

items.name: Create or import
items.text: Register an existing directory, or clone a git URL (file URLs included).

items.name: Assign teams
items.text: Attach one or more teams to a project, and archive, restore or delete it later.

items.name: Per-project permissions
items.text: Override the default permission profile for one project's conductor.

items.name: Start and stop a conductor
items.text: Each project can run a conductor that coordinates its teams. It always starts with full autonomy and orchestration enabled.

items.name: Pin the conductor's account
items.text: Choose the account, model and profile the conductor is born on. Restart the conductor for a change to take effect.

items.name: Dispatch by preference
items.text: A bound queue first, then a fitting role on the project's team, then the global pool, and a direct spawn only as a last resort. The reply says what actually happened.

items.name: Live sessions and checkpoints
items.text: The project screen shows live sessions, checkpoints and its setup settings in one place.

figure.alt: Projects: a project bound to teams and a task queue, live sessions, checkpoints and the per-project setup/conductor-account settings.
figure.caption: Actual Chimera interface · demo data

categories.title: Roles with per-team overrides
categories.label: Roles
categories.short: Reusable settings, with per-team overrides you can see
categories.keywords: role library binding override pinned inherited instructions model effort permission skills plugins mcp allowlist template
categories.problem: Copying the same instructions, model and tool limits into every spawn drifts quickly, and one tweak for one team should not change every other team.
categories.benefit: Define a role once in a library. Teams bind it, inherit its fields and pin only what differs. The editor shows which values are inherited and which are overridden.
categories.scenario: A reviewer role in the library uses a careful model and read-only tools. The Atlas team binds it and pins a different working directory. Other teams keep inheriting the library value.

items.name: What a role holds
items.text: Model, effort, permission profile, instructions, plugins, skills, an MCP tool allowlist, account, turn limits, isolation and worker pool size.

items.name: Templates, not live agents
items.text: Editing a role changes future spawns, not agents already running from it. The form says how many are live.

items.name: Inherited versus pinned
items.text: For each field the editor shows the library value in grey as inherited, or the pinned override highlighted, with a toggle between them.

items.name: Editable any time
items.text: Overrides can be edited after a role is already bound, without a separate edit mode.

items.name: Provenance badges
items.text: Team members show where each role setting comes from.

figure.alt: Roles: the role library beside team role bindings, with a binding's override editor showing which fields are pinned vs inherited.
figure.caption: Actual Chimera interface · demo data

categories.title: Teams that share a queue
categories.label: Teams
categories.short: Named groups of agents with a shared queue and concurrency
categories.keywords: team members concurrency queue worker pool role binding live workers ask team my team cwd
categories.problem: A handful of agents with no structure step on each other and nobody knows who is free.
categories.benefit: A team is a named group of role-bound workers tied to a queue with a concurrency cap. Work is routed to a free worker of the right role.
categories.scenario: The Atlas team has a developer and a reviewer role and a cap of two concurrent workers. Push five tasks and two start; the rest wait their turn, and the team view shows who is working on what.

items.name: Members and roles
items.text: Create a team with a role, a maximum concurrency, a working directory and an optional queue and purpose.

items.name: Live workers
items.text: The team view lists its workers and what they are doing.

items.name: Edit in place
items.text: The same form edits an existing team.

items.name: Assign by team and role
items.text: Route a task to a free or idle worker of a role through the team's queue, or to one agent directly.

items.name: Team-aware messaging
items.text: An agent can see its own team and message the whole team.

figure.alt: Teams: the 'atlas' team with its bound queue, members, role provenance badges, pinned vs inherited role settings and live workers.
figure.caption: Actual Chimera interface · demo data

categories.title: Queues with priorities and dependencies
categories.label: Queues
categories.short: Prioritized tasks with dependencies and retries
categories.keywords: queue task priority fifo dependency depends on retry pause resume cancel move edit requeue explain why not running remediation gate
categories.problem: A pile of tasks in a chat window has no order, no memory of what depends on what, and no answer to why something is not running.
categories.benefit: Queues order work by priority and arrival, hold tasks until their dependencies finish, retry failures, and tell you exactly why a task has not started.
categories.scenario: On Atlas, a tests task depends on a refactor task. You add a late dependency instead of writing run this last in a prompt. The tests task stays blocked, and an explain call names the unmet dependency.

items.name: Priority then first-in
items.text: Priority breaks ties among ready tasks; arrival order does the rest.

items.name: Dependencies are constraints
items.text: A task will not run until what it depends on is done, and cascades to failed if a dependency fails. Self-dependencies and cycles are rejected.

items.name: Pause and resume
items.text: Stop dispatch from a queue without losing its tasks.

items.name: Edit, move, cancel, retry, requeue
items.text: Fix a pending task, move it between queues, cancel it, or retry a failed one.

items.name: Retries
items.text: Failed tasks retry under a bounded policy.

items.name: Why is this not running?
items.text: One call evaluates the scheduler's own ordered checks: team binding, queue paused, task state, dependencies, drain order, role, concurrency, workflow binding and spawn limits. It names the first one that blocked.

items.name: Remediation jumps backward
items.text: A step configured for remediation can request a bounded jump to an earlier step with a correction brief when the real root cause is upstream.

items.name: A default gate workflow
items.text: Queued tasks run through a gated workflow by default.

figure.alt: Chimera team queue for the Atlas website demo: done, running, pending and blocked tasks, with the selected task's dependsOn inspector (demo data)
figure.caption: Actual Chimera interface · demo data

categories.title: Workflows with real gates
categories.label: Workflows
categories.short: Multi-step plans with gates, fan-out and loops
categories.keywords: workflow dag gate fan-out join loop sub-workflow plan critic evaluator approval shell artifact check route condition step journal studio
categories.problem: Agents say they are done. Without an independent check, done only means stopped talking.
categories.benefit: Describe the steps as a graph and gate each one on something that can fail: a command, an artifact, a human approval or a critic loop.
categories.scenario: The Atlas release workflow builds, fans out three reviewers, joins their findings and waits at a human approval gate. If the test command fails, the task loops back to the fix step a bounded number of times and then stops for you.

items.name: A graph of steps
items.text: Steps form a DAG with routing conditions, bounded loop-back, fan-out and join, and sub-workflows.

items.name: Plan a workflow from a goal
items.text: A planning step can design the workflow at runtime and compile it as a sub-workflow, under the same gate, checkpoint and budget rules.

items.name: Four kinds
items.text: A shell command, an artifact check, a human approval, or an evaluator-optimizer critic loop.

items.name: On failure
items.text: Retry, loop back, or request remediation from an earlier step.

items.name: Workflow studio
items.text: Create, edit, run and inspect workflows in the app.

items.name: A durable step journal
items.text: One entry per step attempt with model, account, tokens, cost, gate outcome and timings. It survives daemon restarts and the queue's terminal-task eviction.

categories.title: Scheduled jobs that survive sleep
categories.label: Schedules
categories.short: Cron, interval and one-shot jobs that run unattended
categories.keywords: schedule job cron interval one-shot timezone overlap catch-up snooze history import export retry dead letter requeue run now wake sleep budget template
categories.problem: Recurring work, like a nightly dependency check, normally means a cron entry on one machine that nobody remembers and nothing records.
categories.benefit: Schedule agent work by cron, interval or once. Each run is recorded with how it was triggered and how it ended, and a laptop that was asleep does not silently lose a run.
categories.scenario: A nightly job on the Atlas team checks for outdated packages at 02:00 in your timezone. The laptop was asleep, so the run is marked late and coalesced. A failed run retries, and after repeated failure lands in the dead letter list until you requeue it.

items.name: Cron, interval, one-shot
items.text: With an explicit timezone, and next-run time shown for each job.

items.name: Three kinds of target
items.text: A team and role, an inline agent definition, or an existing agent that is resumed if paused. A killed or missing target disables the job.

items.name: Prompt templates
items.text: Use the job name, timestamp, ISO time or agent id in the prompt.

items.name: Overlap policy
items.text: Decide what happens when a run is still going at the next tick.

items.name: Catch-up
items.text: Optionally run a missed occurrence if it is not staler than a limit you set.

items.name: Sleep and wake
items.text: Runs that come due while the machine slept coalesce unless wake is enabled on macOS. Sleep-wake runs record how late they were.

items.name: Budget ceiling per job
items.text: Cap what one run may spend.

items.name: Retries and dead letter
items.text: A bounded retry budget, then a dead-letter state. Requeue revives a dead-lettered job, resets its retries and re-arms the next occurrence.

items.name: Run now and snooze
items.text: Fire a job on demand, or snooze it until later.

items.name: Run history
items.text: Each run records whether it was scheduled, manual or catch-up, and whether it was ok, failed or skipped.

items.name: Import and export
items.text: Move a schedule definition between installs.

figure.alt: Queues → schedules: jobs with cron/interval cadence, next run and last result, plus the selected job's run history (scheduled, manual, catch-up; ok/failed/skipped).
figure.caption: Actual Chimera interface · demo data

categories.title: Shared memory the whole fleet can search
categories.label: Memory
categories.short: Shared notes with ranked search, graphs and pins
categories.keywords: memory note decision fact todo question wiki link backlink folder tag pin search semantic lexical graph chronicle index
categories.problem: Every new agent starts from zero. What one agent learned on Monday is gone by Tuesday, and the next agent repeats the mistake.
categories.benefit: Agents and people write notes, decisions, facts, todos and questions into one shared store, and search it by meaning or by keyword before starting related work.
categories.scenario: An Atlas agent records a decision that the site uses system fonts only. A week later another agent searches memory before touching the stylesheet, finds the decision, and follows it.

items.name: Kinds
items.text: Note, decision, fact, todo and question.

items.name: Folders, tags and pins
items.text: Organize notes in folders, label them with tags and pin the ones that matter.

items.name: Backlinks
items.text: Wiki-style links connect notes, and linked-from lists appear on each one.

items.name: Hybrid search
items.text: Lexical and semantic search together.

items.name: Scope is ranking
items.text: Scoping a search changes ranking. It is not access control.

items.name: Your own history
items.text: An agent can search the record of its own past turns after its context was compacted.

items.name: Graph
items.text: A graph of links and dangling references; semantic edges appear only once the vector index is ready.

items.name: Capacity and index status
items.text: See how full memory is and whether the semantic index is built.

figure.alt: Chimera shared memory: notes by folder with pins and tags, and the selected note's links and backlinks (demo data)
figure.caption: Actual Chimera interface · demo data

categories.title: Artifacts and checkpoints
categories.label: Artifacts and checkpoints
categories.short: Keep what agents produce and snapshot a tree without touching HEAD
categories.keywords: artifact checkpoint revert snapshot design file output gate check restore
categories.problem: Agents produce files and plans that get lost in a transcript, and a bad edit has no easy way back.
categories.benefit: Register the outputs that matter as artifacts the workflow can check, and take checkpoints you can roll a working tree back to.
categories.scenario: An Atlas agent registers a plan artifact. The workflow gate checks that it exists before the build step. A later edit goes wrong, so you revert the working tree to the last checkpoint.

items.name: Add, list, read
items.text: Agents register named outputs and read them back later.

items.name: Usable as gate checks
items.text: A workflow step can require that an artifact exists.

items.name: Revisions in the design workspace
items.text: Snapshots of artifact revisions can be browsed there, and the selected one pinned.

items.name: Create and list
items.text: Take a checkpoint of a working directory and see them in the project view.

items.name: Revert
items.text: Hard-reset a working tree to a prior checkpoint.

items.name: Never touches your history
items.text: Checkpoints do not change HEAD, the index or git history.

categories.limits: A revert is a hard reset of that working tree; use it on purpose.

categories.title: Review, evidence and worktrees
categories.label: Review and worktrees
categories.short: A human check with evidence before work lands, plus worktree leases
categories.keywords: review room diff finding decision evidence provenance merge commit worktree isolation lease handoff single writer land
categories.problem: Agent changes arrive as a pile of edits. Reviewing them means hunting for branches, diffs and the reason a change exists.
categories.benefit: Every agent works in its own git worktree. A review room shows the diff, findings and the decision, and an evidence panel traces a change from branch to diff to merge commit.
categories.scenario: An Atlas worker finishes in its own worktree. In the review room you add a finding on one hunk, the worker fixes it, and you approve. The evidence panel then links the branch, the diff and the merge commit.

items.name: Live diff
items.text: The diff refreshes while the task is still in progress.

items.name: Findings and decision
items.text: Add and resolve findings, then decide. The decision button guards against double-submit.

items.name: Changes and evidence
items.text: A panel traces provenance branch, then diff, then merge commit.

items.name: One worktree per agent
items.text: Created with git worktree under a per-key directory so concurrent agents do not edit the same files.

items.name: Single-writer lease
items.text: One agent holds the write lease for a worktree. Leases can be listed, handed off or released; a release while the holder is still live needs force.

categories.limits: Worktrees isolate changes, not processes or filesystem access. An agent with full permissions can still reach outside its worktree.

categories.title: MCP store with trust and OAuth
categories.label: MCP store
categories.short: MCP servers with trust levels, OAuth and discovery
categories.keywords: mcp store server trust untrusted full oauth bearer import discovery proxy direct session shared exclusive http proposal built-in laya browser desktop package ownership exclusive session proposal http
categories.problem: Every MCP server you add is code with access to your agent. Wiring them into each client by hand leaves nothing you can review.
categories.benefit: One store holds every MCP server. An agent's proposal arrives disabled and untrusted, and agents can propose servers but cannot enable, trust, add credentials to or sign in to them. Calls to an untrusted server that can write ask first.
categories.scenario: An Atlas agent proposes an HTTP MCP server it found. It appears in Settings as a disabled, untrusted proposal. You review it, sign in with OAuth yourself and mark it trusted. Until you enable it, agents cannot call its tools. The daemon may still run its guarded, unauthenticated OAuth metadata check to see how the server signs in, and the sign-in itself stays a human step.

items.name: Disabled and untrusted proposals
items.text: An agent's proposal and a package installed from the store are saved disabled and untrusted. Servers imported from Claude or Codex config come in enabled and fully trusted. Either can be changed afterwards. Trust is full or untrusted, and unknown means untrusted.

items.name: Approval on risky calls
items.text: A call to an untrusted server that may write asks for approval. Calls the server hints are read-only are allowed.

items.name: Reviewed packages
items.text: Package-based servers are reviewed before install, with lifecycle scripts off.

items.name: Built-in servers
items.text: Chimera's own browser and desktop servers and the Laya server are built in and cannot be uninstalled.

items.name: Import from Claude and Codex
items.text: Find the servers already configured in those clients and import them. Imports arrive enabled and fully trusted, so look them over, and switch trust down for any you want approvals on.

items.name: OAuth discovery
items.text: For a remote URL you add or import, the daemon makes an unauthenticated request for public OAuth metadata through an SSRF guard: public addresses only, redirects re-checked, time and size bounded. If it finds an authorization server the entry defaults to OAuth. This can happen while the server is disabled, and an inconclusive result never blocks the add. A localhost or LAN server is stored but not auto-detected, so choose its auth type yourself. The same public-only rule holds when an untrusted entry, such as an agent's proposal, signs in. A fully trusted entry may use private addresses, and so may the live connection of any server you enable, so a local MCP server keeps working.

items.name: Agents can propose
items.text: An agent's proposal is a disabled, untrusted entry for you to review. It cannot enable or trust it, add headers or credentials, or complete OAuth, and it does not install a package.

items.name: OAuth and bearer
items.text: HTTP servers use bearer tokens or OAuth, with a status chip and a re-authorize action.

items.name: Session modes
items.text: Share one session, give each agent its own, or take it exclusively.

items.name: Direct or proxy-only
items.text: Choose whether agents see a server's native tools or reach them only through the proxy.

items.name: Chimera as an MCP server
items.text: Claude Code, Codex or any stdio MCP client can drive Chimera through its MCP server. A small core of tools (spawn, wait, send, ask, memory, team basics) is always visible; the rest are found and called on demand, so their schemas are not sent on every turn.

items.name: One tool surface out
items.text: The same store connects Chimera out to other MCP servers, so agents reach one set of tools instead of every client configuring the same servers.

figure.alt: Settings → MCP store: built-in servers (no uninstall) beside external servers, each with a trust badge (full/untrusted) and an OAuth status chip (authorized, needs re-auth, bearer, never); hosts are reserved example domains.
figure.caption: Actual Chimera interface · demo data

categories.title: A secrets manager with grants and an audit trail
categories.label: Secrets manager
categories.short: Named secrets with per-agent grants and an audit trail
categories.keywords: secret secrets keychain grant inject reveal audit redaction environment variable credential token
categories.problem: Agents need tokens, and pasting them into prompts or committing them next to the code puts them in logs and transcripts.
categories.benefit: Store a secret once, grant it to specific agents in a mode you choose, and have every read audited. Values are stored in the system keychain.
categories.scenario: The Atlas deploy agent gets a deploy token in inject mode: it appears as an environment variable the next time the agent starts. A review agent gets reveal mode and has to read it through the secret tool, which writes an audit entry each time.

items.name: System keychain
items.text: Values go to the system keychain. The secrets file holds only names, descriptions and grants, never values, and is private to your user.

items.name: Names, not values, in the UI
items.text: The settings screen shows names, descriptions and masked state.

items.name: Inject or reveal
items.text: Inject sets an environment variable at the agent's next start. Reveal lets the agent read the value through a tool.

items.name: Uniform denial
items.text: An agent that is not granted a secret, one that is granted inject only, and a secret that does not exist all look the same.

items.name: Agents list only their own grants
items.text: An agent cannot enumerate secrets it was not given.

items.name: Audit
items.text: Writes, grants and reads are recorded, with allow or deny for grants and reads.

items.name: Redaction
items.text: A value an agent revealed is registered for redaction in logs.

items.name: Operator-only management
items.text: Setting, deleting, granting and revoking are not exposed to agents through MCP.

categories.limits: On macOS the value is passed to the keychain command as an argument, so it is briefly visible to other local processes. A corrupt secrets file makes the daemon refuse to start rather than guess.

figure.alt: Settings → Secrets: named secrets with descriptions and per-agent grant modes; values are never shown, only names and masked state.
figure.caption: Actual Chimera interface · demo data

categories.title: Browser and desktop control, with a monitor
categories.label: Computer use
categories.short: Browser, desktop control and optional Laya assistance
categories.keywords: computer use browser headless desktop control laya macos lease monitor stop screenshot preview exclusive
categories.problem: An agent that can click and type on your machine is powerful and risky, and you need to see what it is doing and stop it.
categories.benefit: Give agents a headless browser or, on macOS, control of the real desktop, optionally with Laya, a local assistant that ranks candidate actions. While an agent holds the desktop, a live preview appears in that agent's own transcript with a Stop button. Desktop control is exclusive, so two agents never fight over the mouse.
categories.scenario: An Atlas agent drives the macOS desktop to check how the staging page renders in your real browser window. A small preview sits at the upper right of that agent's transcript with the target window and the latest actions. When one looks wrong, you press Stop desktop control.

items.name: Laya (optional)
items.text: Optional local action-ranking assistance for computer use. It needs macOS 14 or later. You install it from the Computer use card, which downloads one English model pinned to a full revision and checked against a digest; after that it runs offline. It is English-only: a multilingual or typed-decision request fails rather than fetching a model Chimera has not reviewed.

items.name: Headless browser
items.text: Browser automation without a window, with its own session for each agent; not supported on Linux arm64 or Windows arm64. The lease and the live preview below belong to desktop control, not to this.

items.name: Desktop control
items.text: Control the real desktop, which an agent has to acquire first. macOS only.

items.name: Exclusive desktop lease
items.text: An agent acquires and releases desktop control, so only one controls it at a time. A call in progress cannot be taken over, and an idle lease expires after five minutes.

items.name: Preview in the owner's transcript
items.text: The monitor sits at the upper right of the transcript of the agent that holds the lease, and only there. It shows the lease owner, whether it is busy, the target window and recent tool outcomes.

items.name: Hide is not Stop
items.text: Hiding or collapsing the preview only pauses the preview; the agent keeps control. Stop desktop control ends it and also turns off automatic startup.

items.name: Not a recorder
items.text: The monitor does not keep screenshots, typed text or call arguments.

categories.limits: The screenshot above is a synthetic demo target, clearly labelled, not a real desktop. Desktop control and Laya are macOS only. Laya only helps rank actions: the exclusive lease and the Stop button apply the same way with or without it.

figure.alt: Agent transcript with the Desktop control monitor (preview + recent actions + Stop button) over a synthetic target image clearly labelled DEMO — not a real desktop.

categories.title: Skills and plugins on demand
categories.label: Skills and plugins
categories.short: Install, enable and bind skills and plugins
categories.keywords: skill plugin discovery search read toggle index context
categories.problem: Loading every skill into every prompt wastes context, and agents rarely know which skill fits the task.
categories.benefit: Agents search the skill index and load a skill at the moment they need it. Plugins can be switched on and off from one card.
categories.scenario: An Atlas agent about to write a test searches skills for testing guidance, reads the one it finds and applies it, without carrying the others in its prompt.

items.name: Search and read
items.text: Agents search for a skill and read it only when needed.

items.name: Scoped to the project
items.text: The index favors the agent's project's own skills first.

items.name: List and toggle
items.text: See plugins and enable or disable them.

items.name: Per-role skills and plugins
items.text: Roles list the skills and plugins their agents get.

categories.title: Event subscriptions and hooks
categories.label: Hooks
categories.short: Rules on daemon events that notify, queue work or run a command
categories.keywords: event subscription hook trigger notify webhook toast os command spawn push topic filter throttle wake
categories.problem: Polling for an event wastes tokens, and reacting to one automatically usually means a custom script.
categories.benefit: An agent can sleep until an event arrives. A hook reacts to an event with no agent in the loop: notify, queue a task, spawn, run a sandboxed command, or send a notification.
categories.scenario: A hook on Atlas pushes a regression-check task whenever code lands on main. A notify rule sends an OS notification when a queue drains, throttled so it does not repeat.

items.name: Wake on an event
items.text: Subscribe, then end your turn. Topics include agent settled or spawned, task state, gate verdict, queue drained, repo landed, memory added, permission or question pending, budget warning, system woke, prompt stalled and job dead-lettered.

items.name: Filters
items.text: Narrow by agent, tree, task, queue, team, state or tags.

items.name: Durable hooks
items.text: Run actions when a matching event fires: notify an agent, push a task, spawn an agent, run a local command or send a notification.

items.name: Channels
items.text: Toast, OS notification or webhook.

items.name: Notify rules
items.text: Event, filter, channel and throttle per rule, with a test button that bypasses the throttle.

items.name: Last fired
items.text: The hooks card shows when a rule last fired or was suppressed.

categories.title: Federation across machines
categories.label: Federation
categories.short: Connect Chimera instances across machines
categories.keywords: federation peer remote machine ssh tunnel pairing invite allow spawn accounts concurrency cloudflare read-only
categories.problem: Sometimes the machine with the repository or the GPU is not the one you are sitting at.
categories.benefit: Pair Chimera installs so one can see another's agents and, only if you allow it, start work there. Peers are read-only by default.
categories.scenario: You pair your laptop with a desktop that holds the Atlas build cache. The peer is read-only until you explicitly allow it to spawn, and then only with the accounts you listed.

items.name: Read-only peers
items.text: Per-peer spawn permission defaults to off. The account allowlist defaults to none, and concurrency is capped.

items.name: Provider keys stay local
items.text: Peers exchange account names, never keys or tokens. Configuration and the account set stay on each machine. The one secret that travels is the single-use pairing token inside the invite.

items.name: SSH-tunneled socket
items.text: Pinned host keys and a dedicated restricted key; optional Cloudflare Access in front.

items.name: Pairing by invite
items.text: The raw token appears only in the invite blob. Lists show hashes, and the host key is pinned on first use.

items.name: Peer status
items.text: A local snapshot of peers' last-known status and cached host-tool summaries.

categories.limits: Federation is the most experimental surface, with little everyday use. It is configured as peers in config, not a single switch.

categories.title: One attention inbox
categories.label: Inbox
categories.short: Questions, approvals and notifications that need you
categories.keywords: inbox attention notification question approval prompt failed blocked ask human escalate toast dedupe
categories.problem: Permission prompts, questions, approvals and failures arrive in different places and the important one is buried.
categories.benefit: A single, prioritized, de-duplicated feed of everything waiting on you, with the actions to resolve it.
categories.scenario: Overnight an Atlas worker asks a question, a gate waits for approval and one task fails. In the morning the inbox lists all three, most urgent first, instead of three tabs.

items.name: Permission prompts
items.text: Pending tool permission requests.

items.name: Questions
items.text: Agents can ask you, another agent or a team, and you answer from the app.

items.name: Approval gates
items.text: Workflow steps waiting for a human.

items.name: Failed and blocked tasks
items.text: So you notice them.

items.name: Prioritized and de-duplicated
items.text: One feed derived from live state.

items.name: Notify rules
items.text: Optional toast, OS or webhook notifications for the events you pick.

categories.title: History, events and diagnostics
categories.label: History and diagnostics
categories.short: Look back at what ran: events, replay and diagnostics
categories.keywords: history events replay diagnostics doctor support report audit chain journal slo health export backfill cost run
categories.problem: When something went wrong last night, chat scrollback does not tell you which run, which model, what it cost or what happened in order.
categories.benefit: One history of everything the fleet ran, an event log you can page through and replay, and diagnostics you can run without starting the daemon.
categories.scenario: A scheduled Atlas job failed overnight. History shows the run, its trigger and its cost. The events screen shows the sequence around it, and you export a sanitized Markdown excerpt for a bug report.

items.name: Run history
items.text: Agents, queue tasks and scheduled firings in one list with trigger, model, cost, outcome and duration. Kind and outcome chips filter it, and it refreshes itself.

items.name: Events
items.text: A full-width event table with paged replay and backfill.

items.name: Agents as of a time
items.text: Reconstruct agent status from the last snapshot plus later events.

items.name: Doctor
items.text: A command that checks your install without starting the daemon.

items.name: Support report
items.text: Privacy-minimized JSON for a bug report.

items.name: Sanitized export
items.text: A bounded Markdown export of retained events from an agent and its sub-agents.

items.name: Audit chain
items.text: Verify the local audit hash chain. Verification reports; it does not repair.

items.name: Performance
items.text: A service-level screen over latency, tokens, cost, gate failures and error rates.

categories.title: A workbench next to the agents
categories.label: Workbench
categories.short: File viewer, in-app terminal, design canvas and command palette
categories.keywords: workbench file viewer terminal dock design workspace command palette keyboard help welcome pin path line highlight resize
categories.problem: Watching agents from one window and reading their files from another breaks your flow.
categories.benefit: Open the file an agent mentioned at the exact line, run a command in an in-app terminal, review design artifacts, and reach supported actions from the keyboard.
categories.scenario: An Atlas agent reports a problem at a file and line. You open it from the transcript with the line highlighted, check something in the in-app terminal below, and move on without leaving the app.

items.name: File tree and viewer
items.text: Open a path, and a path with a line number scrolls to and highlights that line.

items.name: In-app terminal
items.text: A resizable dock. While it has focus, every keystroke belongs to it.

items.name: Agents and the terminal
items.text: An agent can read and write a terminal you opened for it.

items.name: Design workspace
items.text: Snapshots of artifact revisions with the selected snapshot pinned.

items.name: Command palette
items.text: Search commands, shortcuts, slash commands, settings and entities from one palette.

items.name: Mouse and keyboard match
items.text: Mouse controls trigger the same actions as their shortcuts.

items.name: Help and welcome
items.text: In-app help and a first-run screen.

advanced.name: Batch send and resume
advanced.text: Message or resume several agents in one call.

advanced.name: Agents can rename themselves
advanced.text: An agent can set its own display name.

advanced.name: Find and tail
advanced.text: Look up agents and read their recent activity.

advanced.name: Write-gate dry run
advanced.text: Ask whether writing given paths would be refused, and which check refused it.

advanced.name: Host tool scan cache
advanced.text: The host CLI tool scan is cached for about fifteen minutes.

advanced.name: Clear a cooldown
advanced.text: One action clears an account's cooldown and releases its session-limit pauses.

advanced.name: Assign versus dispatch
advanced.text: Assign targets an agent or a team and role. Dispatch follows the project's routing preference.

advanced.name: Cycle-safe dependencies
advanced.text: Adding a dependency to a pending task rejects self-dependency and cycles.

advanced.name: Step journal filters
advanced.text: Filter the journal by task, agent, step, queue, team or outcome.

advanced.name: Sleep-wake records
advanced.text: A run that fired late after sleep records its trigger and how late it was.

advanced.name: Dead-letter event
advanced.text: A dead-lettered job raises an event you can subscribe to.

advanced.name: Memory pressure events
advanced.text: Events fire when memory is under pressure or when notes are evicted.

advanced.name: Index status
advanced.text: Check whether the vector index is built before relying on semantic links.

advanced.name: Corrupt file fails closed
advanced.text: A corrupt secrets file stops the daemon instead of silently losing grants.

advanced.name: Remove, list, call
advanced.text: List, add and remove servers, inspect their tools and call a tool through the store.

advanced.name: Importable servers
advanced.text: List what could be imported before importing it.

advanced.name: Force-release a lease
advanced.text: Release a worktree lease even while its holder is live, only on purpose.

advanced.name: Tag filters
advanced.text: Match a task's tags in a hook or subscription filter.

advanced.name: Event search export bound
advanced.text: An export is capped at a fixed number of events and does not write files.

advanced.name: Chronicle
advanced.text: Semantic search over your own agent's past turns, commands and results.

advanced.name: Pins
advanced.text: Pin a task or an agent so its live fields stay in view.

advanced.name: Agent-to-agent history
advanced.text: An overlay of agent messages opens from the command palette.
